title: Python for the labs, part 1: arrays, waves, and plots
summary: Read and write the code in Koo's notebooks yourself: make a time axis, turn a wave formula into one line of numpy, and draw it with matplotlib (labels, zoom, several panels). Every step runs right here and checks your answer.
sourceNote: Built from the code in LING 124 Labs 1 to 6 (ling124_lab1 to lab6.ipynb): the sinusoid() and plot_sinusoid() helpers from Lab 2, the subplot grids from Labs 1, 2 and 6, the time slices from Lab 1. Every code cell runs in the app.

blocks.md: Every LING 124 lab notebook does the same few things over and over: **make a time axis**, **make a wave** (or load a sound), **cut out a piece**, **plot it**, and later **take its FFT**. This chapter teaches each of those moves as a few lines of Python, one at a time.

The grey boxes with a **Python** tag are real code. Click **Run** (or press Cmd+Enter) and it runs right here, no Colab needed. Boxes marked **Your turn** also check your answer the moment you run it and tell you exactly what's off. The first run takes about 10 seconds while Python loads; after that it's instant.

rows: `import numpy as np` and `import matplotlib.pyplot as plt`
The first cell of every lab

blocks.title: The six moves
Your first run
blocks.task: Click **Run**. The first line loads numpy and gives it the short name `np`, which is why every lab writes `np.something`.
blocks.starter:
import numpy as np

print("Python is working.")
print("pi is", np.pi)

sections.heading: numpy arrays: a list you can do math on

blocks.body: A row of numbers that numpy treats as one thing. When you do math to an array, it happens to **every number at once**. You make one with `np.array([...])` or `np.arange(n)`.

blocks.title: A plain list vs. an array
blocks.body:
Plain Python list:  [1, 2, 3] * 2   gives  [1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3]   (it repeats the list)
numpy array:        np.array([1, 2, 3]) * 2   gives  [2 4 6]   (it doubles every number)
blocks.answer: Signals are arrays, so `x * 2` doubles the loudness of the whole wave in one step.

blocks.title: See the difference yourself
blocks.task: Run it and compare the two printed lines.
blocks.starter:
import numpy as np

plain = [1, 2, 3]
arr = np.array([1, 2, 3])

print("list * 2  :", plain * 2)
print("array * 2 :", arr * 2)
print("array + 10:", arr + 10)

blocks.body: The array `0, 1, 2, ..., n-1`: **n numbers, starting at 0**, never reaching n itself. It's how every lab counts samples.

blocks.title: Your turn: math on a whole array
blocks.task: Make `a` the array `[0, 0.5, 1]`. Then make `b` equal to **3 times a, plus 1**, in one line (no loop).
blocks.starter:
import numpy as np

a = None   # replace None
b = None   # replace None

print(b)
blocks.check:
import numpy as np
assert a is not None and b is not None, "Replace both `None`s with real code."
assert isinstance(a, np.ndarray), "`a` should be a numpy array: use `np.array([0, 0.5, 1])`."
assert np.allclose(a, [0, 0.5, 1]), f"`a` should be [0, 0.5, 1]. Yours is {a}."
assert np.allclose(b, [1, 2.5, 4]), f"`b` should be [1, 2.5, 4]. Yours is {b}. Remember: 3 * a + 1."
blocks.solution:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([0, 0.5, 1])
b = 3 * a + 1

print(b)
hints: An array is made from a list: `np.array([0, 0.5, 1])`.
Write the math exactly as you'd say it: `3 * a + 1`. numpy applies it to every number.
blocks.success: `3 * a + 1` ran on all three numbers at once. That's the whole trick of numpy, and it's why `A * np.cos(...)` can build a whole wave in one line.

blocks.md: Getting numbers out works like lists: `x[0]` is the first, `x[-1]` is the last, and `x[2:5]` is positions 2, 3, 4 (the end number is **not** included).

blocks.title: Your turn: pick numbers out
blocks.task: `idx` is the array 0 to 9. Make `first3` hold the first three numbers and `last2` the last two. Use slices, not typed-out numbers.

first3 = None   # replace None
last2 = None    # replace None

blocks.check:

assert first3 is not None and last2 is not None, "Replace both `None`s."

last2 = idx[-2:]

hints: `idx[:3]` means "from the start up to (not including) position 3".
`idx[-2:]` means "from the second-to-last to the end".
blocks.success: Slices are how Lab 1 cuts the two "per" syllables out of the recording. Same syntax, just with sample numbers.

blocks.body: Powers are `**`, not `^`. In Python `2 ^ 3` is 1 (a bitwise trick), not 8. Write `x ** 2` for x squared.
Forgot the `np.`? `cos(t)` gives **NameError: name 'cos' is not defined**. numpy's functions always start with `np.`: `np.cos`, `np.pi`, `np.abs`.

sections.heading: The time axis: turning sample numbers into seconds

blocks.body: How many samples (measurements) per second. `fs = 16000` means 16,000 numbers for every second of sound.
The time, in seconds, of every sample. Sample number n happens at **n / fs** seconds. So `t = np.arange(N) / fs`.

blocks.title: fs = 1000, first 5 samples
blocks.body:
sample numbers n:  0      1      2      3      4
t = n / fs:        0.000  0.001  0.002  0.003  0.004  seconds

blocks.md: How many samples is a duration? **duration × fs**. Half a second at 16,000 Hz is 0.5 × 16000 = 8000 samples. That's why Lab 2's helper starts with this exact line:

blocks.title: From Lab 2's sinusoid()
blocks.body: t = np.arange(int(duration * sampling_rate)) / sampling_rate
blocks.answer: Count the samples, number them 0 to N-1, divide by fs to get seconds.

blocks.title: Your turn: build a time axis
blocks.task: Make the time axis for **0.1 seconds at fs = 1000 Hz**. First set `n_samples`, then `t`.
blocks.starter:
import numpy as np

fs = 1000
duration = 0.1

n_samples = None   # how many samples?
t = None           # the time of each sample, in seconds

print(n_samples, t[:3], t[-1])
blocks.check:
import numpy as np
assert n_samples is not None and t is not None, "Replace both `None`s."
assert int(n_samples) == 100, f"0.1 s at 1000 samples per second is 100 samples. You have {n_samples}."
assert len(t) == 100, f"`t` should have 100 values. Yours has {len(t)}."
assert abs(t[1] - 0.001) < 1e-12, f"The second sample should be at 0.001 s. Yours is at {t[1]}. Did you divide by fs?"
assert abs(t[-1] - 0.099) < 1e-12, f"The last sample should be at 0.099 s (not 0.1: counting starts at 0). Yours is {t[-1]}."
blocks.solution:
import numpy as np

fs = 1000
duration = 0.1

n_samples = int(duration * fs)
t = np.arange(n_samples) / fs

print(n_samples, t[:3], t[-1])
hints: Samples = duration × fs. Wrap it in `int(...)` so it's a whole number.
`np.arange(n_samples)` gives 0, 1, ..., 99. Divide that by `fs`.
blocks.success: The last time is 0.099 s, not 0.1, because the numbering starts at 0. That's also why Lab 2 Q12 ("how many samples in 0.1 s?") is duration × fs.

blocks.body: Always wrap the sample count in `int(...)`. `0.3 * 16000` is `4800.000000000001` on a computer, and `np.arange` of that gives 4801 samples, one too many. `int()` cuts it back to 4800.

sections.heading: Making a wave from its formula

blocks.md: Once you have `t`, a wave is one line. Each piece of the formula maps to one piece of code:

rows: The wave shape (works on a whole array)
The time axis you just built
Where the cycle starts, in radians
blocks.title: x(t) = A cos(2πFt + ϕ)
Lab 2's wave: x(t) = 2 cos(2π·100·t + π/3)
blocks.body: x = 2 * np.cos(2 * np.pi * 100 * t + np.pi / 3)
blocks.answer: Read left to right: amplitude 2, frequency 100 Hz, phase π/3.

Copy the formula piece by piece from the table: `2 * np.cos(2 * np.pi * 100 * t + np.pi / 3)`.

blocks.body: A reusable recipe with a name. `def sinusoid(...):` defines it, the lines pushed in by 4 spaces are the recipe, and `return` hands the result back. Lab 2 starts by defining `sinusoid()` so each question is one short call.

blocks.title: Your turn: write Lab 2's sinusoid() yourself
blocks.task: Finish the function so it returns the time axis `t` and the wave `x` for any amplitude, frequency, phase, duration, and sampling rate. The last two lines call it.
blocks.starter:
import numpy as np

def sinusoid(amplitude=1, frequency=10, phase=0, duration=1.0, sampling_rate=16000):
    t = None   # the time axis
    x = None   # the wave
    return t, x

t, x = sinusoid(amplitude=2, frequency=100, phase=np.pi/3, duration=0.1)
print(len(t), x[0])
blocks.check:
import numpy as np
t1, x1 = sinusoid(amplitude=3, frequency=50, phase=0, duration=0.02, sampling_rate=1000)
assert t1 is not None and x1 is not None, "Inside the function, replace both `None`s."
assert len(t1) == 20, f"sinusoid(duration=0.02, sampling_rate=1000) should give 20 samples. Yours gave {len(t1)}. Use the function's own `duration` and `sampling_rate`, not fixed numbers."
assert np.allclose(x1, 3 * np.cos(2 * np.pi * 50 * np.arange(20) / 1000)), "The time axis is right, the wave isn't. Use `amplitude`, `frequency` and `phase` (the names in the parentheses) in the formula."
t2, x2 = sinusoid()
assert len(t2) == 16000, "Called with no arguments, it should use the defaults: 1 second at 16000 Hz."
blocks.solution:
import numpy as np

def sinusoid(amplitude=1, frequency=10, phase=0, duration=1.0, sampling_rate=16000):
    t = np.arange(int(duration * sampling_rate)) / sampling_rate
    x = amplitude * np.cos(2 * np.pi * frequency * t + phase)
    return t, x

t, x = sinusoid(amplitude=2, frequency=100, phase=np.pi/3, duration=0.1)
print(len(t), x[0])
hints: Inside the function, use the names from the first line (`duration`, `sampling_rate`, `amplitude`, ...), not fixed numbers.
The two lines are the time-axis line and the wave line from before, with names instead of numbers.
blocks.success: This is Lab 2's exact helper. Now `sinusoid(frequency=-100, ...)` or `sinusoid(sampling_rate=500, ...)` in the aliasing questions is just you calling your own function.

blocks.body: `np.cos` wants **radians**. A phase of 60° must be written `np.pi / 3`, not `60`. If a lab says π/3, type `np.pi / 3`.

sections.heading: Plotting: figure, axes, plot, labels, show

blocks.body: The whole picture, like one sheet of paper.
One graph drawn on that sheet: its own x-axis, y-axis, lines and labels. A figure can hold several.

blocks.md: Every plot in the labs is these steps:

rows: Make a sheet (10 wide, 3 tall) with one graph on it
Draw a line through the points (t, x): time across, amplitude up
Title above the graph (Lab 1 writes `ax.title.set_text(...)`, same thing)
Zoom the x-axis to 0 to 0.01 s
Draw a horizontal line at 0 (Lab 2's dotted center line)
blocks.title: The plotting calls from the labs
Try it: Lab 2's plot
blocks.task: Run it. Then change `frequency=100` to `200` and run again: twice as many cycles fit in the same 0.02 s.
blocks.starter:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fs = 16000
t = np.arange(int(0.02 * fs)) / fs
x = 2 * np.cos(2 * np.pi * 100 * t + np.pi / 3)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3))
ax.plot(t, x)
ax.axhline(0, linestyle='dotted', color='black')
ax.set_xlabel('time (s)')
ax.set_ylabel('amplitude')
plt.show()

blocks.body: `plt.plot(...)` and `ax.plot(...)` both draw, but mixing them draws on whichever graph was made last. With more than one panel, always use the `ax` you mean.
Makes a grid of graphs. Now `ax` is a **list of axes**, not one axes: `ax[0]`, `ax[1]` for one column, `ax[row, col]` for a grid.

sections.heading: Cutting out a piece by time

blocks.md: To grab the stretch from 0.4 s to 0.6 s, turn each time into a **sample number** (time × fs), then slice. This is exactly Lab 1's code for the first "per":

blocks.title: Lab 1
blocks.body:
start_1 = int(0.4 * fs); end_1 = int(0.6 * fs)
interval_1 = x[start_1:end_1]
# its own time axis, for plotting:
np.arange(start_1, end_1) / fs
blocks.answer: Seconds × fs = sample number. Slice with those numbers.

blocks.title: Your turn: cut 0.25 s to 0.5 s
blocks.task: `x` is a 1-second signal at `fs = 8000`. Make `piece` = the samples from **0.25 s to 0.5 s**, and `t_piece` = their times in seconds.
blocks.starter:
import numpy as np

start = None     # sample number at 0.25 s
end = None       # sample number at 0.5 s
piece = None
t_piece = None

print(len(piece), t_piece[0], t_piece[-1])
blocks.setup:
import numpy as np
fs = 8000
_t = np.arange(fs) / fs
x = np.cos(2 * np.pi * 220 * _t) * np.exp(-2 * _t)
blocks.check:
import numpy as np

blocks.solution:
import numpy as np

start = int(0.25 * fs)
end = int(0.5 * fs)
piece = x[start:end]
t_piece = np.arange(start, end) / fs

print(len(piece), t_piece[0], t_piece[-1])
